questions.prompt: What is meant by the **carrying capacity** of an environment?

choices.text: The maximum population of a species that the environment can support in the long term
The number of species living in the environment
The fastest rate at which a population can grow
The total mass of all organisms in the environment

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity, $K$, is the maximum population size that the available resources can sustain over time. In the logistic model, growth stops when $N = K$.
Density-dependent factors have a bigger effect when a population is crowded, so they regulate it around $K$. Drought and eruptions affect the population whatever its density.

questions.prompt: In a capture–mark–release–recapture study, 80 beetles are caught, marked and released. A week later 60 beetles are caught, and 15 of them are marked. Estimate the size of the beetle population.
A population grows logistically with $r = 0.5$ per year and carrying capacity $K = 1200$. Calculate the population growth rate $\frac{dN}{dt}$, in individuals per year, when $N = 300$.
What is the name of the square frame, often 1 m × 1 m, placed at random positions to sample plants?
questions.explanation: A **quadrat** marks out a known area. Counting the individuals in many randomly placed quadrats lets you estimate density and total population.

questions.prompt: Ecologists record the numbers of a predator and its prey in a national park over many years. Both populations rise and fall in cycles. Explain why the cycles happen and why the predator peaks come after the prey peaks.
questions.marking_guide: 1 mark: when prey are plentiful, predators have more food, so more survive and breed and predator numbers rise. 1 mark: more predators eat more prey, so prey numbers fall. 1 mark: with less prey, predators starve or breed less, so predator numbers fall, allowing prey to recover and the cycle to repeat. 1 mark: predator peaks lag behind prey peaks because predators take time to respond, as breeding and growth of young take time, so predator numbers keep rising for a while after prey start to fall.
questions.explanation: Predator and prey numbers are linked by negative feedback: prey numbers control predator food supply, and predator numbers control prey deaths. The delay in the predators' breeding response makes their peaks lag behind.
